items.name: Body text hits 4.5:1
items.check: Compute the ratio for every text/background pair actually rendered — body, muted, placeholder, disabled, badge — and confirm each clears 4.5:1, or 3:1 for text at 24px+ or 18.66px+ bold.
items.why: WCAG 1.4.3. Below 4.5:1 the words are physically unresolvable for low-vision users and for anyone reading on a phone in daylight — the copy ships but the message never lands.
items.antiPattern: #999 on #FFF body copy (2.85:1) shipped because it 'looked cleaner' on a calibrated studio monitor in a dim room.
items.fix: Darken the foreground token until the computed ratio clears 4.5:1 — measure it with `uikit.mjs --contrast`, never by eye. Muted text is a contrast decision, not a lightness decision.

items.name: Controls and icons hit 3:1
items.check: Confirm every input border, toggle track, checkbox outline, chart gridline that carries meaning, and every meaning-bearing icon reaches 3:1 against the surface directly behind it.
items.why: WCAG 1.4.11. If a control's boundary is invisible, the user cannot find the thing they are supposed to operate — the text being readable does not help if the box around it isn't.
items.antiPattern: 1px #E5E7EB borders on white inputs (1.24:1) — the field is invisible until it's clicked, so the form reads as a list of floating labels.
items.fix: Raise the border token to at least 3:1 for interactive elements. Purely decorative dividers may stay lighter — the rule follows meaning, not the element name.

items.name: Focus is always visible
items.check: Tab through the whole screen and confirm every stop paints an indicator that is at least 2px thick and at least 3:1 against the colour it sits on — including inside modals, menus and custom controls.
items.why: WCAG 2.4.7 / 2.4.11. Without a focus ring a keyboard user is navigating blind: they can move, but they cannot know what they are about to activate.
items.antiPattern: `outline: none` in a global `*` reset with nothing put back, because the default ring 'looked ugly' on one button.
items.fix: Delete the blanket reset. Use `:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--ring); outline-offset: 2px }` — pointer users never see it, keyboard users always do.

items.name: Everything works without a mouse
items.check: Unplug the mouse and complete the primary flow end to end — every control reachable by Tab in a sane order, activatable with Enter or Space, and no point where Tab cannot get back out.
items.why: WCAG 2.1.1 / 2.1.2. Keyboard operation is the substrate every switch device, screen reader and voice-control tool sits on — break it and you break all of them at once.
items.antiPattern: `<div onClick>` styled as a button: no tab stop, no role, no Enter handler — it works perfectly for the developer testing with a mouse and is invisible to everyone else.
items.fix: Use a real `<button>`. If it truly must be a div it needs role, tabindex=0, and Enter+Space handlers — three things the native element gives you free.

items.name: Icon-only controls have names
items.check: Confirm every icon-only button, link and toggle exposes an accessible name — aria-label, visually-hidden text, or a title on an SVG — that names the action rather than the glyph.
items.why: WCAG 4.1.2 name/role/value. A screen-reader user hears 'button, button, button' and has no way to know which one deletes their data.
items.antiPattern: A row of pencil / duplicate / trash icon buttons in a table, each announcing as an unlabelled 'button'.
items.fix: `<button aria-label="Delete invoice 1042">` — name the outcome, not the picture. 'Trash icon' tells the user nothing about what is about to be destroyed.

items.name: Inputs are programmatically labelled
items.check: Confirm every input, select and textarea is bound to its label via `for`/`id` or aria-labelledby — verify in the accessibility tree, not by looking at the design.
items.why: WCAG 1.3.1 / 4.1.2. Visual proximity means nothing to a screen reader: an unassociated field announces as 'edit text, blank' and the user is typing into an unnamed box.
items.antiPattern: A `<span>` styled to look like a label sitting above an input, with no `for` — it reads correctly to the eye and is silent to the accessibility tree.
items.fix: `<label for="email">` + `<input id="email">`. As a bonus the label becomes part of the click target, which makes the field easier to hit on touch.

items.name: Images carry the right alt
items.check: Confirm every `` has an alt attribute: describing the information if the image carries any, and `alt=""` if it is purely decorative — with none missing the attribute entirely.
items.why: WCAG 1.1.1. A missing alt makes the screen reader fall back to reading the filename; a wrong alt makes decorative noise out of what should be silence.
items.antiPattern: `alt="image"` on everything, so a product page announces 'image, image, image', and decorative flourishes announced as 'graphic' between every paragraph.
items.fix: Ask what the user would lose if the image vanished — that answer IS the alt. Nothing lost means `alt=""`. Never `alt="photo of"` — the screen reader already says 'image'.

items.name: Structure is real HTML
items.check: Confirm the screen uses header/nav/main/footer landmarks, has exactly one h1, and descends heading levels without skipping — then read the generated heading outline and check it makes sense alone.
items.why: WCAG 1.3.1 / 2.4.6. Screen-reader users navigate by jumping between headings and landmarks; without them the only route through the page is to listen to all of it, top to bottom.
items.antiPattern: A page built entirely from nested `<div>`s where headings are styled spans — the heading list comes back empty and 'skip to content' has nothing to skip to.
items.fix: Pick the tag for its meaning and style it afterwards. Heading level is document structure, not a font-size picker — use CSS for the size.

items.name: Colour is never the only signal
items.check: View the screen in greyscale and confirm nothing is lost — required fields, errors, status badges, active states and inline links all still readable without hue.
items.why: WCAG 1.4.1. Roughly 8% of men cannot separate your red from your green; and colour is the first thing lost to a dim screen, a cheap projector, or a printout.
items.antiPattern: A required field marked only by a red label, and inline links distinguished from body copy by colour alone with `text-decoration: none`.
items.fix: Pair every colour signal with a second channel — an icon, a border, a weight change, a word. Colour is an accelerator for people who can see it, never the carrier.

items.name: Dialogs manage focus
items.check: Open every modal, drawer and popover from the keyboard and confirm focus moves inside on open, cannot Tab out to the page behind, and returns to the element that opened it on close.
items.why: WCAG 2.4.3 / 2.1.2. Without focus management a screen-reader user opens a dialog and is still standing outside it, tabbing through a page that is visually covered and functionally gone.
items.antiPattern: A modal that renders on top visually while focus stays on the trigger — Tab walks invisibly through the page underneath, and Esc does nothing.
items.fix: Use the native `<dialog>` element or a maintained primitive (Radix, React Aria). Hand-rolled focus traps miss Shift+Tab, portals, and the return-focus case.

items.name: Status messages are announced
items.check: Confirm anything that appears without a focus change — toasts, 'saved', result counts, validation summaries — sits in a live region (role=status or role=alert) that existed in the DOM before the message did.
items.why: WCAG 4.1.3. A confirmation nobody hears is a confirmation that did not happen: the screen-reader user is left unsure whether their action worked, so they do it again.
items.antiPattern: A success toast injected into the DOM with the live region created in the same render — the region is announced, the text inside it is not.
items.fix: Render the empty live region on mount and write text into it later. role=status for informational, role=alert for errors that interrupt.

items.name: Tap targets reach 44x44
items.check: Measure the hit area of every tappable control and confirm it reaches 44x44 CSS px — 24x24 is the WCAG 2.2 AA floor, 44 is the platform norm — even where the visible glyph is smaller.
items.why: WCAG 2.5.8; Apple HIG 44pt; Material 48dp. A fingertip is roughly 45px of contact area — below that the user is aiming at something they cannot see under their own thumb.
items.antiPattern: A 16x16 close 'x' in a modal corner: pixel-hunting on a phone, and every miss costs the user the form they were filling in.
items.fix: Keep the icon 16px and grow the hit area with padding or a `::before` overlay — the target expands, the visual does not.

items.name: Targets don't crowd each other
items.check: Confirm adjacent tap targets are separated by at least 8px of dead space, and that no destructive action sits within a thumb-width of a routine one.
items.why: Size alone does not prevent mis-taps — two 44px buttons flush against each other still produce wrong hits, and the cost of the wrong hit is what matters.
items.antiPattern: 'Save' and 'Delete' rendered as flush neighbours in a table row, so a slightly low tap destroys the record the user meant to keep.
items.fix: 8px minimum between neighbours; separate destructive actions entirely — different region, or behind an overflow menu.

items.name: Every input answers in 100ms
items.check: Confirm every tap, click and keypress produces a visible state change within 100ms — pressed state, spinner, optimistic update or disabled — before any network call resolves.
items.why: 100ms is the threshold where an interface stops feeling connected to the finger. Past it users assume the tap missed and try again — which is how you get three identical orders.
items.antiPattern: A submit button that looks identical for two seconds while the request flies, so the user taps it three more times.
items.fix: Paint the pressed/loading state synchronously in the event handler, not inside the promise's `.then()`. And disable the control while it is in flight.

items.name: Nothing hides behind hover
items.check: Confirm every action reachable by hover is also reachable by tap and by keyboard focus — no menu, tooltip, or row control that exists only on `:hover`.
items.why: Touch devices have no hover state, and neither does a keyboard. A hover-only control is not 'harder' on a phone — it does not exist.
items.antiPattern: A nav dropdown that opens on hover only: on touch the first tap navigates to the parent, so the submenu is permanently unreachable.
items.fix: Bind the same disclosure to click and focus as well as hover. Row actions that fade in on hover must stay visible on touch — check with a coarse-pointer media query, not the viewport width.

items.name: Gestures always have a button
items.check: Confirm any action driven by swipe, drag, pinch or long-press has an equivalent single-tap path that is visible without performing the gesture first.
items.why: WCAG 2.5.1. Path-based and multipoint gestures exclude anyone with limited dexterity or a switch device — and a gesture is invisible, so most users never learn it exists.
items.antiPattern: Swipe-to-delete as the only delete: undiscoverable to new users, impossible with a tremor, and unreachable from a keyboard.
items.fix: Keep the gesture as the accelerator for people who find it, and put the same action in the row's overflow menu for everyone else.

items.name: Destruction is recoverable
items.check: Confirm every destructive action either asks for confirmation naming the specific object, or completes immediately with an Undo affordance that lasts at least five seconds.
items.why: Users act faster than they read. The design has to make the mistake recoverable, not merely warned about — a warning nobody reads is decoration.
items.antiPattern: 'Are you sure?' with OK/Cancel and no object name, so the user confirms out of muscle memory and deletes the wrong record.
items.fix: Prefer optimistic delete plus an 'Undo' toast: faster for the 99% who meant it, and genuinely safer for the 1% who didn't. Reserve modals for the truly unrecoverable, and name the object in the button: 'Delete 3 invoices'.

items.name: Clickable things look clickable
items.check: Confirm every interactive element is distinguishable from static content without hovering it — by shape, weight, underline or colour-plus-a-second-cue — and that `cursor: pointer` never appears on non-interactive text.
items.why: An affordance discovered by accident is an affordance most users never discover. They do not sweep the mouse across the page looking for things that light up.
items.antiPattern: Flat 'ghost' text buttons that are visually identical to labels, found only when a user happens to drag across them.
items.fix: Give every control a resting visual boundary — background, border, or underline. Hover is confirmation, never the reveal.

items.name: Scroll behaves like scroll
items.check: Confirm wheel and touch scrolling are not intercepted, that no custom inertia or snap fights the OS, and that nested scroll containers hand the scroll back at their edges instead of trapping it.
items.why: Scrolling is the one gesture every user has fully internalised. Overriding it makes the page feel broken in a way people cannot articulate — they just leave.
items.antiPattern: Full-page scroll-jacking that animates exactly one section per wheel tick, so a single trackpad flick skips three sections and lands nowhere.
items.fix: Let the browser scroll. If you need section snapping, use CSS `scroll-snap-type: y proximity` — it cooperates with the OS instead of replacing it.

items.name: LCP lands under 2.5s
items.check: Measure Largest Contentful Paint on a throttled 4G / mid-tier Android profile and confirm it lands under 2.5s — on the real deployed URL, not localhost.
items.why: Core Web Vitals threshold. Past 2.5s a meaningful share of users abandon before the page has said anything at all, and the work behind the page never gets seen.
items.antiPattern: A 3MB hero JPEG that is the LCP element AND carries `loading="lazy"`, so it only starts downloading after the JS bundle parses.
items.fix: Find the actual LCP element first (it is usually the hero image or the h1), then give it `fetchpriority="high"`, a preload, and no lazy attribute. Optimising anything else is guessing.

items.name: CLS stays under 0.1
items.check: Confirm Cumulative Layout Shift stays under 0.1: images and video carry width/height or aspect-ratio, ads and embeds get reserved boxes, and web fonts swap into a metric-matched fallback.
items.why: A page that moves while you read it is a page that makes you lose your place — and occasionally makes you tap the wrong thing because the button arrived where your finger already was.
items.antiPattern: Text renders, then an image above it loads and shoves the paragraph the user was mid-sentence through off the screen.
items.fix: Always set intrinsic dimensions, even on responsive images — width/height give the browser the aspect ratio, CSS still controls the rendered size.

items.name: Async regions reserve their space
items.check: Confirm every async region reserves its final dimensions before the data arrives — skeletons shaped like the real content's box, not a centred spinner in a collapsed div.
items.why: The jump when data lands is the most jarring shift on the page, because it happens exactly when the user has started reading what was already there.
items.antiPattern: A 40px spinner in an auto-height container that resolves into a 600px table — the entire page below it lurches.
items.fix: Skeletons should be the same shape and count as the content they stand in for. A skeleton that is the wrong height is just a slower layout shift.

items.name: INP stays under 200ms
items.check: Confirm Interaction to Next Paint stays under 200ms — no single block of synchronous work over 50ms inside a click, input or keypress handler.
items.why: Core Web Vitals threshold. A frozen input is worse than a slow page: the page was never promising to be instant, but the text field was.
items.antiPattern: Filtering a 10,000-row table synchronously inside `onChange`, so every keystroke locks the input for 300ms and characters arrive in bursts.
items.fix: Move the work off the keystroke: debounce, `useDeferredValue`/transitions, a worker, or a virtualised list. Paint first, compute second.

items.name: Images are sized and modern
items.check: Confirm images ship as AVIF or WebP with a responsive srcset, encoded no larger than 2x their largest rendered box — no 2000px asset painted into a 320px slot.
items.why: Images are usually 60-80% of a page's bytes. Every unnecessary kilobyte is paid for by the user on their data plan, on their battery, in their time.
items.antiPattern: A PNG screenshot exported at 4x from Figma — 2.4MB — rendered 300px wide, because it 'looked crisp'.
items.fix: `srcset` + `sizes`, AVIF with a WebP fallback. Use the framework's image component if there is one; it does the encoding and the sizing that you will otherwise forget.

items.name: Lazy-load below the fold only
items.check: Confirm everything below the fold — images, iframes, heavy components, third-party embeds — defers, and that nothing above the fold does.
items.why: Lazy-loading is a targeted tool. Applied indiscriminately it delays exactly the content the user is waiting for, making the page measurably slower while the code looks more optimised.
items.antiPattern: `loading="lazy"` applied to every image including the hero, adding a full round-trip to LCP.
items.fix: Fold-line rule: above it, eager and prioritised; below it, lazy. A YouTube embed above the fold should be a click-to-play poster image, not an iframe.

items.name: First-load JS has a budget
items.check: Confirm first-load JS for the critical route stays near 150KB gzipped, with charts, editors, date pickers and maps dynamically imported at the point of use.
items.why: JS is the most expensive byte on the page: it must be downloaded, parsed, and executed on the main thread, and a mid-tier phone does that an order of magnitude slower than your laptop.
items.antiPattern: A date library with every locale, plus a charting package, in the main bundle — for a route that renders one chart below the fold.
items.fix: Look at the bundle analyser output before optimising anything else. The win is almost always one dependency, not a hundred small savings.

items.name: Web fonts never hide text
items.check: Confirm web fonts are self-hosted, subset, preloaded, and use `font-display: swap` with a size-adjusted local fallback so no text is ever invisible while a font loads.
items.why: Flash of invisible text means the user stares at a blank page that has already finished rendering — the content arrived, the font decided not to show it.
items.antiPattern: Three weights pulled from a third-party CDN with default `font-display: block`, giving up to 3s of invisible text on a slow connection plus an extra DNS lookup and TLS handshake.
items.fix: Self-host, subset to the glyphs you use, preload the one weight above the fold. Tune `size-adjust` and `ascent-override` on the fallback so the swap doesn't also cause a layout shift.

items.name: No emoji standing in for icons
items.check: Confirm no emoji is used as a UI icon in navigation, buttons, headings, or status — emoji appear only inside user-generated content.
items.why: Emoji are font glyphs owned by the OS: they render as a different picture on every platform, ignore your colour tokens, sit on the text baseline instead of the icon grid, and get announced as 'rocket' by a screen reader.
items.antiPattern: A rocket emoji as the deploy button's icon, and a checkmark emoji as the success state — the two most-photographed pixels in the product, drawn by Apple.
items.fix: Use the project's icon set; the rocket exists in Lucide. Emoji as icons is the single fastest visual tell that a UI was generated rather than designed.

items.name: Icons come from one family
items.check: Confirm every icon comes from a single family at a consistent stroke width, size and optical weight — no mixing outline with filled, or one library with another.
items.why: Icon sets encode a drawing style — corner radius, stroke, terminal shape. Two sets in one screen reads as two products stapled together, even to users who could never name the cause.
items.antiPattern: Outline icons in the nav, filled icons in the toolbar, one Font Awesome leftover in the footer, and a 3D illustration in the empty state.
items.fix: Pick one set and take its gaps as a constraint. Drawing one missing icon in the house style beats importing a second library for it.

items.name: One component, real variants
items.check: Confirm each control exists once with declared variants (primary/secondary/ghost, sm/md/lg) and that no screen has hand-built its own version with a different height, radius, or shadow.
items.why: Forked components drift silently: the fix lands in one, the other keeps the bug, and the product slowly stops looking like one thing built by one team.
items.antiPattern: Six visually different 'primary' buttons across five screens, because each was rebuilt locally when the shared one didn't quite fit.
items.fix: When the shared component doesn't fit, add a variant to it — don't fork it. If the variant list is getting long, that is information about the design, not about the code.

items.name: Spacing comes off one scale
items.check: Confirm every margin, padding and gap is a step on one scale (4px base: 4/8/12/16/24/32/48/64) with no arbitrary 13px or 27px nudges.
items.why: Off-scale spacing reads as sloppiness to users who could never articulate why — and it turns every future change into a manual re-nudge of forty hand-tuned values.
items.antiPattern: `margin-top: 17px` tuned by eye until it 'looked right', repeated across the app with forty slightly different values.
items.fix: If a step on the scale looks wrong, the problem is usually the element's own padding or line-height, not the gap. Fix the cause rather than adding a value to the scale.

items.name: Radius and elevation are finite
items.check: Confirm corner radius and shadow are drawn from a small defined set — roughly three radii and three elevations — assigned by role rather than per-component taste.
items.why: Radius and shadow are how a UI communicates depth and grouping. Randomised, they stop meaning anything and the interface reads as noisy rather than layered.
items.antiPattern: A 4px-radius card containing a 12px-radius input beside a fully-round button, each with a different hand-tuned shadow.
items.fix: Nest radii coherently: an inner element's radius should be the outer radius minus the padding, or the corners visibly disagree.

items.name: Dark mode is authored
items.check: Confirm dark mode is an authored token set with its own verified contrast — surfaces lightening with elevation, shadows replaced by lighter surfaces or borders — not an inversion or an opacity trick.
items.why: Inverted dark mode turns brand colours into their opposites and photos into negatives. It also silently breaks contrast: a pair that passed in light frequently fails once inverted.
items.antiPattern: `filter: invert(1)` on the root, which renders the brand blue as mustard and every product photo as an X-ray.
items.fix: Never pure black (#000) — use an elevated near-black around #0A0A0B and lighten surfaces as they rise. Desaturate accents slightly; a colour that sang on white will vibrate on black.

items.name: Button labels name the outcome
items.check: Confirm every button label is a verb phrase naming what will happen ('Create invoice', not 'Submit' or 'OK'), and that the same action uses the same word everywhere in the product.
items.why: A label that names the outcome lets the user decide without reading the dialog body — which they were never going to read anyway.
items.antiPattern: 'OK' on a dialog asking 'Discard changes?' — OK to discard, or OK to keep? The user has to guess, and half of them guess wrong.
items.fix: Make the buttons answer the question the title asks: 'Discard changes?' → 'Discard' / 'Keep editing'. Never 'Yes'/'No' on a destructive prompt.

items.name: Pinch-zoom always works
items.check: Confirm the viewport meta has no `user-scalable=no` and no `maximum-scale` below 5, and that the layout still works at 200% browser zoom and reflows without loss at 400%.
items.why: WCAG 1.4.4 / 1.4.10. Pinch-zoom is the most-used accessibility feature on earth — most people using it don't consider themselves disabled, they just have forty-year-old eyes.
items.antiPattern: `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, maximum-scale=1, user-scalable=no">` copied from a 2013 template to stop iOS zooming on input focus.
items.fix: `width=device-width, initial-scale=1` and nothing else. If you were disabling zoom to stop the input-focus jump, the real fix is a 16px font size on the input.

items.name: Nothing scrolls sideways at 320px
items.check: At a 320px viewport, confirm the document body never scrolls sideways: no fixed-px element wider than the viewport, long strings and URLs wrap or truncate, and wide tables or code blocks scroll inside their own container.
items.why: Body-level horizontal scroll takes the whole layout with it — the nav and the sticky CTA slide off too, and the user has to pan back to find them.
items.antiPattern: A 400px-wide table forcing the entire document to pan, discovered only after launch because nobody tested narrower than their own phone.
items.fix: Give the wide child `overflow-x: auto`; never let the body do the scrolling. Track it down with `* { outline: 1px solid red }` rather than guessing.

items.name: Built narrow, then widened
items.check: Confirm the base stylesheet is the narrow layout and breakpoints add complexity upward with min-width — then verify the result at 320, 768, 1024 and 1440px.
items.why: Desktop-first inverts the effort: the hardest constraint gets handled last, by subtraction, and the majority of real traffic gets the layout nobody designed.
items.antiPattern: A desktop grid written first with max-width overrides bolted on, so the phone receives a squeezed four-column layout with 9px gutters.
items.fix: Let content decide the breakpoints, not device names. Add one where the layout starts to look wrong — iPhone widths are not a design system.

items.name: Layout survives real content
items.check: Render every layout with the worst realistic content — a 60-character name, a three-line title, a zero state, a 200-item list, and a translated string 40% longer than the English.
items.why: Designs are drawn with 'Item 2' and shipped against 'Wireless Noise-Cancelling Over-Ear Headphones (Refurbished)'. The layout that only holds for the mock is a layout that breaks on day one.
items.antiPattern: A card grid where every title was two words in the mock, so the real catalogue produces cards of four different heights and a ragged grid.
items.fix: Decide per field: wrap, clamp with `-webkit-line-clamp`, or truncate with a title attribute. Never let it be decided by accident.

items.name: Tables have a narrow-screen plan
items.check: Confirm every data table has a deliberate narrow-screen strategy — a card list, priority columns, or an isolated horizontal scroller with a sticky first column — rather than a shrunken font.
items.why: A table is a two-dimensional comparison; a phone gives you one dimension. Something has to give, and if you don't decide what, the browser decides badly.
items.antiPattern: `font-size: 9px` so all eleven columns technically 'fit' on a phone.
items.fix: Rank the columns by what the user actually scans for. Two or three matter on mobile; the rest belong behind a row tap.

items.name: Respect the safe area and the thumb
items.check: Confirm primary actions sit within the bottom thumb arc on mobile, and that fixed bottom bars pad by `env(safe-area-inset-bottom)` so the home indicator never covers them.
items.why: The top corners of a modern phone are a two-handed stretch. Putting the primary action there makes every use of the app slightly worse, forever.
items.antiPattern: A sticky CTA flush to the viewport bottom, half-swallowed by the iPhone home bar — and a 'Done' button in the top-right of a 6.7-inch screen.
items.fix: `padding-bottom: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-bottom))`. Test in landscape too, where the insets move to the sides.

items.name: Sticky chrome has a budget
items.check: Confirm fixed and sticky chrome — header, cookie bar, promo strip, bottom nav — together consume no more than about a quarter of a 667px-tall viewport.
items.why: Every pixel of permanent chrome is taken from the content the user came for, on the device that has the least of it to give.
items.antiPattern: Sticky header + cookie banner + promo strip + bottom nav, leaving a 300px letterbox to read a long article through.
items.fix: Pick one persistent bar. Let the header hide on scroll-down and return on scroll-up; the promo strip should scroll away and never come back.

items.name: Body text starts at 16px
items.check: Confirm body text renders at 16px or larger, that nothing sustained drops below 14px, and that every form input is at least 16px on mobile.
items.why: 16px is the browser default because it is the researched comfortable reading size. Below 16px on an input, iOS Safari also auto-zooms on focus and re-lays out the page under the user's finger.
items.antiPattern: 13px body copy because the mock was drawn at 1.5x zoom, plus 14px inputs that make the whole page lurch on every tap.
items.fix: Set the base on `html` and size everything in rem, so a user who raised their browser's default font size actually gets it.

items.name: 1.5 line-height, 65ch measure
items.check: Confirm body copy uses roughly 1.5 line-height across a 45-75 character measure, with headings tightening to 1.1-1.25 as they grow.
items.why: WCAG 1.4.12 sets 1.5 as the text-spacing floor. Long unleaded lines make the eye lose its place on the return sweep — the reader doesn't blame the design, they just stop reading.
items.antiPattern: `line-height: 1` on a paragraph spanning a full 1600px window, so every line return is a small act of navigation.
items.fix: `max-width: 65ch` on prose containers. Line-height should shrink as font-size grows — 1.5 on a 48px headline looks like a gap, not leading.

items.name: Components use tokens, not hex
items.check: Confirm components reference semantic tokens (--background, --foreground, --primary, --destructive) with no raw hex, no `text-[#3B82F6]`, and no `bg-blue-500` outside the token definitions themselves.
items.why: Raw values are how a design system dies. The token is the single place a theme change can happen once — without it, dark mode is forty edits and one of them gets missed.
items.antiPattern: #3B82F6 pasted into forty components, so the rebrand takes a week and three screens keep the old blue for a year.
items.fix: Name tokens by role, never by appearance: `--destructive`, not `--red`. The day destructive becomes orange, a token called `--red` is a lie you cannot rename.

items.name: A finite type scale
items.check: Confirm font sizes come from a defined scale (12/14/16/18/20/24/30/36/48), that no screen uses more than five or six of them, and that hierarchy is carried by size and weight rather than colour alone.
items.why: Hierarchy works by contrast between levels. Six near-identical heading sizes produce no hierarchy at all — just six things that are all slightly different for no reason.
items.antiPattern: 17px, 19px and 23px invented per component, giving six heading levels the reader cannot rank.
items.fix: If two levels need to be distinguished, make them clearly different — a 2px gap is noise. Ratios (1.25, 1.333) generate a scale that already knows this.

items.name: Text on images stays legible
items.check: Confirm text over photos or gradients sits on a scrim, solid plate, or gradient overlay that guarantees 4.5:1 against the worst pixel behind it — not the average one.
items.why: WCAG 1.4.3 applies over images too, and the image is the variable you don't control: it renders perfectly on the stock photo and vanishes on the one the customer uploads.
items.antiPattern: A white hero headline over an unscrimmed photo — flawless with the launch image, unreadable the moment marketing swaps in a bright one.
items.fix: A linear-gradient scrim from transparent to rgba(0,0,0,0.6) behind the text block. Guarantee the floor rather than trusting the asset.

items.name: Each status colour means one thing
items.check: Confirm each semantic colour carries exactly one meaning product-wide — destructive is the only red, success the only green — and that no decorative element borrows a status colour.
items.why: Users learn a product's colour language in minutes and then trust it. One decorative red breaks that contract, and afterwards every red has to be read rather than recognised.
items.antiPattern: A green 'Delete' button because the brand is green — the colour says safe, the label says destroy, and the colour wins.
items.fix: If the brand colour collides with a status colour, the status wins inside the UI. Move the brand to surfaces and marketing where nothing depends on it.

items.name: Reduced motion is honoured
items.check: Confirm a `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block removes transforms, parallax and auto-playing motion — keeping opacity fades or nothing — and verify it by actually toggling the OS setting.
items.why: WCAG 2.3.3. For a user with a vestibular disorder, large-scale motion produces genuine nausea and dizziness. This is not a stylistic preference, it is a symptom.
items.antiPattern: The media query exists but only sets `animation-duration: 0.01ms` on `*` — the parallax hero still moves on scroll, because scroll-linked motion isn't an animation.
items.fix: Reduced means remove the movement, not speed it up. Cross-fade instead of slide, and kill scroll-linked transforms entirely — they are not covered by a duration override.

items.name: Transitions land in 150-300ms
items.check: Confirm UI transitions land between 150 and 300ms — enter around 200-300, exit around 150-200 — and that nothing the user must wait through exceeds 400ms.
items.why: Motion is a tax paid on every single interaction. Past roughly 300ms it stops reading as responsive and starts reading as lag — delightful once, infuriating by the fifth time.
items.antiPattern: An 800ms 'premium' page transition that demos beautifully and is the first thing power users ask you to remove.
items.fix: Exits are faster than entries: the user has already decided. Use ease-out for entering, ease-in for leaving, and never linear on anything a human looks at.

items.name: Animate transform and opacity only
items.check: Confirm animations touch only transform and opacity — never width, height, top, left, or margin — and that anything moving is promoted with will-change or a 3D transform.
items.why: Transform and opacity are composited on the GPU. Everything else re-runs layout and paint on every frame, which is the difference between 60fps and a 12fps stutter on a mid-range phone.
items.antiPattern: Animating `height: auto` on an accordion, forcing a full layout pass sixty times a second so the panel judders open.
items.fix: For an accordion, animate `grid-template-rows: 0fr → 1fr`, or transform a fixed-height inner wrapper. Remove `will-change` when the animation ends — left on, it permanently costs memory.

items.name: Motion teaches something
items.check: Confirm every animation answers what it teaches the user — where a thing came from, what changed, or that the system heard them — and delete the ones with no answer.
items.why: Motion with no message is a delay with a personality. It costs the user time on every interaction and buys them nothing they can use.
items.antiPattern: Fade-in-on-scroll on every section, so a fast scroll shows an empty page and Ctrl+F finds text the user cannot see.
items.fix: Motion earns its place by showing continuity: a modal that grows from the button that opened it explains itself. A section that fades in because it entered the viewport explains nothing.

items.name: Nothing moves forever unpausably
items.check: Confirm no video auto-plays with sound, no animation loops for more than five seconds in the periphery, and that anything moving on its own has a visible pause control.
items.why: WCAG 2.2.2. Peripheral motion is involuntarily attention-grabbing — for a user with ADHD or low vision it makes the rest of the page genuinely unreadable.
items.antiPattern: An auto-rotating hero carousel that advances while the user is halfway through reading slide one, and cannot be stopped.
items.fix: Auto-advance is almost always the wrong default — carousels are clicked past, not read. If it must rotate, pause on hover and focus, and give it a real stop button.

items.name: Animation never blocks input
items.check: Confirm nothing blocks interaction while animating: entry animations don't delay interactivity, and the user can click through or interrupt any transition already in flight.
items.why: An animation the user has to wait out converts your polish into their latency. They already know what they want — the interface is the only thing not ready.
items.antiPattern: A modal with a 400ms scale-in that swallows clicks until the animation finishes, so the first tap on the confirm button does nothing.
items.fix: Never gate handlers behind `onAnimationEnd`, and keep `pointer-events` live throughout. A second click should retarget the animation, not queue behind it.

items.name: Labels stay visible while typing
items.check: Confirm every field shows a label that remains visible while the field has content — the placeholder is never the only label.
items.why: Placeholders vanish exactly when the user needs them: on focus. Anyone who is interrupted mid-form comes back to a grid of filled boxes with no idea what any of them are.
items.antiPattern: A placeholder-only form where the user reaches field four, forgets what field two wanted, and has to clear it to read the hint again.
items.fix: Label above the field. Float-labels are acceptable only if the floated state still clears 4.5:1 and stays at 12px or larger — most implementations fail both.

items.name: Errors appear at the field
items.check: Confirm validation errors render next to the offending field, name what is wrong and how to fix it, and are wired to the input via aria-describedby with aria-invalid set.
items.why: WCAG 3.3.1 / 3.3.3. An error the user cannot locate is the same as no error at all — they just see the form refuse to submit and eventually give up.
items.antiPattern: A red 'Please correct the errors below' banner at the top of a twenty-field form, with nothing indicating which field.
items.fix: Say what and how: 'Card expired — check the expiry date', not 'Invalid input'. On submit, move focus to the first bad field so keyboard and screen-reader users are taken there.

items.name: No silent disabled submit
items.check: Confirm no submit button is disabled without telling the user what is missing — prefer an enabled button that reveals the errors when clicked.
items.why: A disabled button is a dead end: it gives no reason, is skipped by screen readers, isn't focusable, and cannot be hovered for a tooltip on touch. The user is stuck with no next move.
items.antiPattern: A greyed-out 'Continue' with no clue which of twelve fields is at fault, and no way to ask.
items.fix: Let them press it and show them what's wrong. If it must stay disabled, put the reason in visible text beside it — not in a title attribute.

items.name: Constraints stated before failure
items.check: Confirm constraints — password rules, accepted formats, max length, file size and type — are stated as helper text before the user types, not revealed by a failed submit.
items.why: A rule the user had no way to know is a trap. They aren't learning your requirements; they're guessing, and each guess costs a round-trip.
items.antiPattern: A password rejected with 'must contain a special character' after submit — a rule that was never shown, on a field the browser has already cleared.
items.fix: Show the rules under the field and tick them off live as they're satisfied. Accept the formats you're going to strip anyway — a phone number with spaces is a valid phone number.

items.name: Validate on blur, not per keystroke
items.check: Confirm fields validate on blur or on submit — never mid-keystroke on a field the user has not finished — and that the error clears the moment the input becomes valid.
items.why: Being told you're wrong while still typing is hostile. The user knows the email is incomplete; they're in the middle of writing it.
items.antiPattern: 'Invalid email address' flashing red after the first character typed into an empty field.
items.fix: Validate late, clear early: first error on blur, then live updates once the field has been touched. Never mark a pristine field invalid.

items.name: Only ask what applies now
items.check: Confirm only the fields that apply right now are visible, that conditional fields appear when they become relevant, and that long forms are chunked into steps with visible progress.
items.why: Every visible field is a reason to abandon. A form's length is the first thing seen and the main thing weighed before starting.
items.antiPattern: A 32-field 'quick signup' showing a company VAT number to individual users, with no indication of how much is left.
items.fix: Cut every field you won't act on this week; ask for the rest later, in context, when the user has a reason to care. The best progressive disclosure is deletion.

items.name: Back does what it says
items.check: Confirm browser and OS back always returns to the previous meaningful view: modals, filters and tab changes push history, and back never ejects the user from a flow or loses their scroll position.
items.why: Back is the user's undo for navigation and the thing they reach for when lost. Breaking it removes their safety net at the exact moment they need it.
items.antiPattern: A full-screen modal that isn't a history entry, so Android's back gesture closes the entire app instead of the dialog.
items.fix: If it changes what fills the screen, it belongs in history. Restore scroll position on back — a list that returns to the top after a detail view makes long lists unusable.

items.name: Every screen has an exit
items.check: Confirm every screen offers a visible way out — close, cancel or back, including full-screen takeovers — and that Esc dismisses any dismissible overlay.
items.why: Feeling trapped is the fastest route to abandonment. Users explore confidently only when they know they can retreat.
items.antiPattern: A full-screen onboarding step with no skip and no close, where the only exit is killing the tab — and the flow starts again on return.
items.fix: Always offer 'Skip'. A user who skips onboarding is still a user; one who closes the tab is not.

items.name: At most five bottom-nav items
items.check: Confirm the bottom or primary nav holds at most five destinations, each a genuine top-level section carrying a text label — and that it never scrolls.
items.why: Past five, targets shrink below the thumb's accuracy and the set stops being memorable — the nav becomes something to read every time instead of something you know.
items.antiPattern: Seven icon-only bottom tabs, one of which is 'More' — the admission that the information architecture was never decided.
items.fix: A 'More' tab is a symptom. If five slots don't fit, the problem is the hierarchy, not the nav.

items.name: Current location is unmistakable
items.check: Confirm the active nav item is marked by more than colour — weight, an indicator bar, or a filled icon — carries `aria-current="page"`, and that the view's title matches the nav label that was clicked.
items.why: 'Where am I' is the question every navigation exists to answer. An indicator only visible to users with good colour vision on a bright screen answers it for some of them.
items.antiPattern: A nav where the current item is 10% darker blue — invisible to a colour-blind user, and to anyone on a dim screen outdoors.
items.fix: Weight or an indicator bar plus colour. And `aria-current` — without it a screen-reader user has no equivalent of the highlight at all.

items.name: Every state has a URL
items.check: Confirm every meaningful state lives in the URL — filters, sort, tabs, pagination, opened detail panes — and that pasting that URL into a fresh tab reproduces exactly what was on screen.
items.why: A state without a URL cannot be shared, bookmarked, reopened, or linked from an alert. The user has to reconstruct it by hand every time, and tell colleagues which five things to click.
items.antiPattern: A dashboard where 'the failing builds view' is reachable only by clicking, so every handoff is a set of verbal instructions.
items.fix: Query params for view state, path segments for identity. Replace rather than push for rapid changes like typing in a filter, or back becomes a keystroke-by-keystroke rewind.

items.name: Labels match where they land
items.check: Confirm nav labels use the user's vocabulary and that clicking one lands on a view whose heading repeats that exact label.
items.why: A mismatch between the label and the destination makes the user wonder whether the click worked. Enough of those and they stop trusting the whole navigation.
items.antiPattern: 'Solutions' leading to a page titled 'Platform', beside invented brand words like 'Nexus' and 'Hub' that must each be clicked to be understood.
items.fix: Name things after what the user is trying to do. If a label needs a tooltip to explain it, it is the wrong label.

items.name: Series readable without colour
items.check: Confirm every data series is distinguishable without colour — direct labels, distinct markers, or dash patterns — by viewing the rendered chart in greyscale.
items.why: WCAG 1.4.1. Around 8% of men cannot separate your red and green series, and every printed, screenshotted, or projected chart is effectively a greyscale chart.
items.antiPattern: A six-line chart whose legend is the only key, in six hues that collapse into four indistinguishable greys.
items.fix: Label lines directly at their right end. A legend is a lookup table the reader has to hold in working memory while their eye travels back to the data.

items.name: Axes labelled and honest
items.check: Confirm both axes carry a label and units, that a bar chart's value axis starts at zero, and that any truncated or logarithmic scale is stated in the chart itself rather than a caption.
items.why: Bar length is the encoding; truncating the axis breaks the proportion the reader is reading. It is the easiest way to mislead people who are trusting you.
items.antiPattern: A bar chart with a y-axis starting at 94%, so a two-point difference is drawn as a tenfold win.
items.fix: Bars must start at zero — their length is the message. Lines may truncate, since they encode change rather than magnitude; say so on the axis.

items.name: Colourblind-safe series palette
items.check: Confirm categorical series colours come from a colourblind-safe ramp (Okabe-Ito, Tableau 10; viridis for sequential), hold 3:1 against the plot background, and stop at about six categories before grouping the tail into 'Other'.
items.why: The default palette of most charting libraries is chosen to look pleasant, not to stay separable — red/green adjacency is the norm rather than the exception.
items.antiPattern: A twelve-category pie in the library's default rainbow, where four of the slices are the same colour to a deuteranopic reader.
items.fix: Beyond six categories, no palette works — group the tail. And never use a rainbow ramp for continuous data; it invents banding that isn't in the numbers.

items.name: Tooltips are never the only channel
items.check: Confirm any value that exists only in a hover tooltip is also reachable another way — direct labels, a companion data table, or keyboard-focusable data points.
items.why: Hover is a desktop-mouse-only channel. On a phone, in a screenshot, or from a keyboard, data that lives solely in a tooltip does not exist.
items.antiPattern: A chart whose numbers appear only on mouse hover, shipped to an audience that reads it mostly on mobile.
items.fix: Label the points that matter — the peak, the current value, the endpoints — directly. Tooltips are for detail on demand, never for the headline number.

items.name: Zero, error and overflow are designed
items.check: Confirm every data surface designs its zero, loading, partial, error and overflow states — including exactly one row and ten thousand rows — not just the happy eight-row mock.
items.why: The empty state is the first thing every new user sees, and the error state arrives on the worst day. Both get skipped because neither appears in the design file.
items.antiPattern: A dashboard that renders an empty axis cross when there is no data — indistinguishable from a broken fetch, so the user reloads and gets the same nothing.
items.fix: An empty state should say why it's empty and what to do next. 'No data' is a status; 'No invoices yet — create your first' is an interface.

items.name: One chart, one question
items.check: Confirm the chart's title states the takeaway as a sentence ('Signups fell 20% after the pricing change') and that the chart type matches the question — no nine-slice pie, no 3D, no dual axis implying causation.
items.why: A chart titled by its variables makes every reader do the analysis again, individually, and reach different conclusions. The point of the chart was to have done it once.
items.antiPattern: 'Metrics Overview' over a 3D exploded pie with twelve slices and a legend, where the reader's job is to find the story you already knew.
items.fix: Write the sentence you want the reader to leave with, then build the chart that proves it. If you can't write the sentence, you don't need the chart.
